name: Nitrate and nitrite poisoning

agents.name: Nitrite (NO2-)
agents.notes: The proximate toxin. Plants accumulate nitrate, and rumen microbes reduce it to nitrite, which is absorbed into the blood, oxidises the ferrous iron of haemoglobin to the ferric form and produces methaemoglobin. Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so the animal effectively suffocates while its blood appears dark brown.

agents.name: Nitrate-accumulating forage and fertiliser
agents.notes: Nitrate accumulates in plants when uptake exceeds the capacity for reduction to protein — typically in drought-stressed plants, after heavy nitrogen fertilisation, or in the rapid growth phase. Cereal crops, brassicas, ryegrass and weeds are the usual sources. Nitrate fertiliser itself is a direct toxic hazard if animals access spills.

hosts.notes: Ruminants are much more susceptible than monogastrics because the rumen converts nitrate to the far more toxic nitrite. Monogastric animals can tolerate higher nitrate intakes, though nitrite itself is still toxic to them. Cattle are the most commonly affected species.

notifiable.note: A plant and fertiliser poisoning with no direct public health significance, though high dietary nitrate is a human food safety consideration in some vegetables.

distribution: Worldwide wherever nitrogen fertiliser is used on forage crops or where drought conditions cause nitrate accumulation. In southern Africa, nitrate poisoning is associated with fertilised pasture, cereal crops and weeds following drought-breaking rains.

aetiology.summary: Nitrate poisoning occurs when forage containing accumulated nitrate is consumed and rumen microbes reduce it to nitrite faster than the animal can metabolise it. The accumulation in plants depends on the balance between nitrogen uptake and the plant's capacity to convert it to protein, which is why drought-stressed and heavily fertilised plants are dangerous.
determinants: Nitrate accumulation in forage, driven by drought stress, fertilisation, low light or rapid growth
Rumen microbial reduction of nitrate to nitrite
The rate of nitrite absorption relative to the rate of its metabolism
The dose consumed, particularly when animals are hungry and eat greedily
risk_factors: Feeding heavily nitrogen-fertilised pasture or hay
Drought-stressed crops and weeds, particularly cereals, brassicas and ryegrass
Sudden grazing of a nitrate-rich crop after a period of feed shortage
Access to nitrate fertiliser, spills or contaminated water
High nitrate water sources, which can be a significant contributor in drought
Low dietary energy, which limits the animal's ability to detoxify nitrite
aetiology.epidemiology: Outbreaks occur when a group is fed or grazed on the same high-nitrate forage, and severity correlates with intake. Cases often follow drought-breaking rain, which triggers rapid regrowth and nitrate accumulation in already-stressed plants. The condition is frequently confused with prussic acid poisoning because both are acute forage-associated intoxications.

pathophysiology.summary: Nitrate is reduced to nitrite in the rumen, and absorbed nitrite oxidises haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen. The result is a functional anaemia: the blood carries less oxygen, the tissues are hypoxic and the animal effectively suffocates. Methaemoglobin also shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve, further impairing oxygen delivery.

cascade.title: Ingestion of high-nitrate forage
cascade.detail: Plants that have accumulated nitrate are consumed, and the nitrate is released into the rumen. Rumen microbial nitrate reductase then reduces nitrate (NO3-) to nitrite (NO2-).

cascade.title: Absorption of nitrite
cascade.detail: Nitrite is absorbed across the rumen wall and into the bloodstream. The rate of absorption depends on rumen pH and the quantity of nitrite produced.

cascade.title: Haemoglobin oxidation
cascade.detail: Nitrite oxidises the ferrous (Fe2+) iron of haemoglobin to the ferric (Fe3+) form, producing methaemoglobin. Methaemoglobin cannot bind oxygen, and the blood takes on a dark brown or chocolate colour.

cascade.title: Impaired oxygen delivery
cascade.detail: Methaemoglobinaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, and the surviving oxyhaemoglobin releases its oxygen less readily. Tissues become hypoxic despite a normal arterial oxygen tension.

cascade.title: Hypoxia, respiratory distress and death
cascade.detail: The brain and heart are most sensitive to hypoxia, producing weakness, rapid respiration, cyanosis, coma and death. Methaemoglobin levels above about 60-70% are usually fatal.

lesions: Dark brown or chocolate-coloured blood that does not brighten on exposure to air
Congestion and oedema of the lungs
Plant material in the rumen consistent with the source
clinical_signs: Rapid, laboured breathing with a normal or slightly increased body temperature
Brown or blue-brown discolouration of the mucous membranes
Cyanosis progressing to a brown-tinged colour in the oral mucosa
Convulsions and coma in severe cases
Sudden death, often within hours of exposure

antemortem: Rapid field test for methaemoglobin in a blood sample — a drop of blood that remains brown rather than turning bright red on exposure to air is highly suggestive
Blood gas or co-oximetry for methaemoglobin percentage where available
Response to methylene blue is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Forage and water analysis for nitrate concentration
postmortem: Dark brown blood and brown-tinged tissues are the characteristic finding
Note the presence of high-nitrate plant material in the rumen
Submit rumen contents and forage for nitrate analysis
laboratory: Methaemoglobin concentration in blood by co-oximetry
Nitrate measurement in plasma, aqueous humour or rumen fluid
A bedside test using a drop of blood on filter paper — brown rather than red indicates methaemoglobinaemia
differentials: Prussic acid (cyanide) poisoning — also acute and forage-associated, but the blood is bright red rather than brown
Carbon monoxide poisoning — similar methaemoglobin-like picture but a different exposure history
Respiratory disease causing hypoxia — fever, cough and abnormal lung sounds
Urea poisoning — ruminants can be poisoned by excess urea; rapid death with severe hyperexcitability
Nitrate fertiliser ingestion — the same mechanism but a direct toxic exposure rather than plant accumulation

prevention: Test nitrate levels in forage before feeding, particularly in drought years
Avoid applying excessive nitrogen fertiliser, especially close to grazing
Do not graze drought-stressed or recently fertilised forage
Dilute high-nitrate forage with low-nitrate roughage
Provide adequate energy in the diet, which improves the rumen's capacity to detoxify nitrite
Secure nitrate fertiliser and prevent animal access
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for a nutritional or fertiliser poisoning.
treatment: Methylene blue (methylthioninium chloride) is the specific antidote — it accelerates the reduction of methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin
Administer slowly intravenously under veterinary supervision, as methylene blue itself can be toxic at high doses
Remove the animal from the source of nitrate immediately
Note that methylene blue is not effective in horses and is not used in that species
outbreak: Remove the offending forage or fertiliser immediately
Submit forage and water samples for nitrate analysis
Treat affected animals with methylene blue
Review fertiliser application and grazing management
Dilute the forage supply or source alternative roughage
public_health: Nitrate poisoning in livestock has no direct public health significance
High nitrate concentrations in drinking water are a human health concern, particularly for infants
Observe meat and milk withdrawal periods for any veterinary medicines used
control.notes: The blood colour is the practical field differentiator: bright red suggests prussic acid, dark brown suggests nitrate. Both are acute forage intoxications and both require immediate removal from the source.

prognosis: Good with prompt methylene blue treatment — animals can recover rapidly and completely. Poor in severe cases with methaemoglobin above 60%, and many animals are found dead. Survivors generally have no lasting effects.
